title: Avere e dire di no
summary: The verb avere, saying no with non, and pointing things out with c'è / ci sono

blocks.title: avere — to have
blocks.body: The other verb you can't live without. **io ho, tu hai, lui/lei ha, noi abbiamo, voi avete, loro hanno.** The *h* is **always silent** — it's just there to keep these forms from looking like other words. *ho* sounds exactly like *o*.

blocks.title: Italian 'has' feelings
blocks.body: Where English *is* hungry/thirsty/right, Italian **has** them: *ho fame* (I'm hungry), *ho sete* (I'm thirsty), *ho ragione* (I'm right), *ho freddo* (I'm cold). Learn these as fixed *avere* phrases — you'll use them daily.

blocks.prompt: How do you say 'I'm hungry' in Italian?
blocks.explain: *Ho fame* — literally 'I have hunger'. Italian uses *avere* for these states.

blocks.title: Saying no: non before the verb
blocks.body: To make a sentence negative, put **non** right before the verb. *Ho tempo* → *Non ho tempo* (I don't have time). *Sono italiano* → *Non sono italiano*. That's it — one word, always just before the verb. No 'do/don't' helper like English.
blocks.callout: *non* + verb. *Non ho fame. Non è vero.*

blocks.prompt: Make it negative: say 'I don't have time.'
blocks.explain: *Non ho tempo.* Just *non* before the verb — nothing else changes.

blocks.title: c'è and ci sono — 'there is / there are'
blocks.body: To say something exists or is present: **c'è** (there is, one thing) and **ci sono** (there are, several). *C'è un bar qui vicino* (there's a bar nearby). *Ci sono due caffè sul tavolo* (there are two coffees on the table). Make it a question just by raising your voice: *C'è un problema?*
blocks.callout: *c'è* = ci + è, one thing. *ci sono* = more than one.

lines.nl: Sì, ci sono due bar in piazza.
lines.en: Yes, there are two bars in the square.

blocks.prompt: Complete: '___ due amici al bar.' (There are two friends at the bar.)
blocks.explain: Two friends = plural, so *ci sono*. *C'è* would be for a single thing.

blocks.prompt: Listen and type. (It means 'Do you have time?')
Write two things you have and one you don't, using avere and non. Add whether there's a bar or a park near you with c'è.
